newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: NZ SPORT, CRICKET - Bizarre incidents inexcusable - Rixon.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT, CRICKET - Bizarre incidents inexcusable - Rixon.

text.p: RAWALPINDI, Nov 29 - New Zealand coach Steve Rixon was unimpressed with a series of bizarre incidents which showcased the eccentricity of Pakistani cricket on the opening day of the second test at Pindi Stadium yesterday, NZPA reports.
The tourists saw out an extraordinary first day on 215 for eight at stumps, a relatively good position after they had been reduced to 111 for seven a little over an hour after lunch.
But the cricket took a back seat to two events which Rixon branded inexcusable.
Firstly, the incompetence of local officials which saw play delayed for 20 minutes while they scurried about trying to find match balls of the required standard.

Another 25 minutes were wasted during the post-tea session when a low lying sun distracted Stephen Fleming and skipper Lee Germon to such an extent that they were forced from the field, delaying their resurrection of New Zealand's innings with what ultimately proved to be a fighting eighth-wicket stand of 81 runs.
Later, fading light saw the players leave the field for a good eight minutes after the 4.30pm local time scheduled close with 17 overs of the day's mandatory 83 overs unbowled.
While Germon saw the funny side of the no-balls fiasco, Rixon didn't, saying it was inexcusable.
"I thought that was very poor, and then the laying of the pitch has to have a bearing on the light situation," Rixon said.
Fleming and Germon had taken the tourists to 181 in four overs after tea, with the lefthanded Fleming on 60 and Germon on 29.
The whole incident left Rixon dumbfounded.
"I could not believe you'd have to leave the ground for something like that in test cricket. That sort of thing should never happen in test cricket.
"But having said that, I can't believe we then had to go back on either. I don't know why we went back and I probably never will.

"I don't see how possibly we could go back on. The sun could only get lower and by doing that get further into the batsmen's eyes. The sun had entered an area whereby it could only get worse," Rixon said.
Pindi Stadium is a relatively new venue and how local officials reached the decision to lay the pitch in its position is beyond comprehension.
Two pavilions stand at opposite ends of the pitch and these must have been built before consideration was given to the logistics of the pitch and the prevailing conditions.
All of this distracted from an intriguing day's play after Pakistan skipper Saeed Anwar asked the Kiwis to bat first.

His decision was vindicated as legspinner Mushtaq Ahmed and rookie fast bowler Mohammad Zahid brewed trouble for the tourists, Mushtaq claiming his seventh five-wicket bag at test level to finish the day with five for 76 from 26 exacting overs.
Zahid, 20, and making his test debut, worked hard and with purpose to impress with three for 51.
Only Fleming and Germon seemed to have the stomach to fight after the middle order of Nathan Astle, Mark Greatbatch, Chris Cairns and Chris Harris buckled, piecing together just 23 runs between them.
Germon joined Fleming in a defiant partnership which saw Fleming post his 10th test half-century and Germon finish the day just five runs short of his maiden test 50.
Fleming was at his languid best on a pitch which played truly until late in the second session when the odd delivery began to skid through.
He looked comfortable against all the Pakistani bowlers, Mushtaq included, until he misread the legspinner's googly to offer a thin edge to wicketkeeper Moin Khan.
Fleming's composed innings contained nine boundaries, mostly square and straight of the pitch.
Germon, who was dropped at slip off occasional slow bowler Salim Malik Malik when he had made 38, offered Fleming the assistance he needed as they got their side out of the doldrums.
He was unbeaten at 45 at the close, just three short of his previous test best and will resume with Dipak Patel, who is on six.
Germon, who later confirmed he would have batted first had he the choice, said his aim was for New Zealand to bat for at least one more hour today (NZ time) and reach 250.
"When I joined Flem it was looking as if we could be bowled out for 150 again or even less. But if we can bat on for another hour tomorrow and post 250 then who knows?" he said yesterday.
Germon said the pitch would get increasingly more difficult to bat on.
"It was very flat to start with but it became lower and powdery. I don't think it will get any easier to bat on. If anything it will deteriorate," he said.
